title: NY State Senate · District 36
area: Bronx neighborhoods including Baychester, Co-op City, Wakefield, Williamsbridge and Woodlawn, plus Mount Vernon in Westchester County.

context.text: The Democratic primary for this seat was canceled; incumbent Jamaal Bailey advanced automatically. Grace Marrero advanced to the general election on the Conservative Party line without appearing on a primary ballot, after also being listed as a withdrawn Republican primary candidate.

candidates.name: Jamaal Bailey
candidates.currentRole: New York State Senator, District 36 (since January 2017)

summary.text: Jamaal Bailey is the Democratic candidate for re-election to New York State Senate District 36, which covers the northern Bronx and the Westchester County city of Mount Vernon. A Bronx native and lawyer who began in politics as an intern and aide to Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, he has been a state senator since January 2017. He chairs the Senate Insurance Committee and the Bronx Democratic Party.

background.text: Born in 1982 and raised in the Bronx, where he attended P.S. 83 in Morris Park, M.S. 181 in Co-op City and Bronx High School of Science; the nysenate.gov biography says he grew up in Wakefield and is a lifelong resident of the district.
Earned a B.A. from the University at Albany, SUNY, and a J.D. from CUNY School of Law.

Began his political career as an intern to Assemblymember Carl Heastie; nysenate.gov says he interned for Heastie during his senior year at Albany and later served as community relations director for Heastie, while Wikipedia describes the role as district director. He also served as a Democratic district leader in the 83rd Assembly District for six years.

Won a five-way Democratic primary on September 13, 2016 for the seat vacated when Senator Ruth Hassell-Thompson resigned to take a position in the Cuomo administration, defeated Conservative Robert Diamond in the November 8, 2016 general election, and was re-elected in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024.
Chair of the Bronx Democratic Party since September 2020, when he succeeded Marcos Crespo.
Chairs the Senate Insurance Committee in the 2025–2026 session, after previously chairing the Senate Codes Committee; his other committees include Codes, Finance, Judiciary and Rules.

According to his nysenate.gov biography, his first term focused on criminal justice measures, including discovery, speedy trial and bail changes enacted in the 2019 budget, and the repeal of Civil Rights Law 50-a on police disciplinary records.

According to nysenate.gov, he is a member of Butler Memorial United Methodist Church and the Williamsbridge Branch of the NAACP, lives in Baychester with his wife and three children, and is a 2026 New York State Senate Veterans' Hall of Fame honoree.

priorities.text: On a bill requiring insurance coverage of speech therapy for stuttering: "We're committed to ensuring every voice, especially those of our youngest, is heard and supported. Stuttering is too often misunderstood and overlooked, and Senate Bill S3654 is a step toward justice in care."

Sponsor's justification for a tenant-eviction bill (S8960-A) notes that "more than 7,500 New York City households have been evicted on days when temperatures exceeded ninety degrees Fahrenheit" since 2017, and proposes barring evictions during dangerously hot or cold weather, or declared weather emergencies.

positions.summary: Sponsors S8960-A, a weather-related tenant protection bill that would bar the execution of residential eviction warrants during dangerously hot or cold weather or declared weather emergencies and for 72 hours afterward.

record.text: Sponsored S3654-A, mandating health-insurance coverage for speech therapy treating stuttering; passed the Senate 57–1 on June 10, 2025, passed both chambers, and was vetoed by the Governor on October 16, 2025.

Sponsored S8960-A, a bill that would bar residential evictions during dangerously hot or cold weather, or weather emergencies; amended and recommitted to the Senate Housing, Construction and Community Development Committee on March 24, 2026, and has not passed either house.
Chairs the Senate Insurance Committee for the 2025–2026 legislative session.

candidates.name: Grace Marrero
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced to the general election on the Conservative Party line without appearing on a primary ballot; also listed as a withdrawn candidate from the Republican primary.

summary.text: Grace Marrero is a retired Bronx native running for New York State Senate District 36 on the Conservative Party line. She was the Conservative Party candidate for State Assembly District 80 in 2024 and for Bronx Borough President in 2025. In her 2024 Ballotpedia survey she describes herself as a community leader and advocate for more than 20 years.

background.text: Born in the Bronx, New York.
Earned a high school diploma from Christopher Columbus High School and a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin in 1980.

Her Ballotpedia profile lists her profession as retired. In her 2024 Candidate Connection survey she describes herself as a mother, grandmother and great-grandmother and a community leader and advocate for the past 20-plus years.
Ran for New York State Assembly District 80 in 2024 on the Conservative Party line, receiving 5.2% of the vote in the general election won by Democratic incumbent John Zaccaro Jr.
Ran for Bronx Borough President in 2025 on the Republican and Conservative Party lines, receiving 17.0% of the vote against incumbent Vanessa Gibson.

priorities.text: "I will fight to repeal bail reform legislation. I will also fight for law enforcement which has been decimated by these laws."
"I will fight to repeal our sanctuary state status."
"My objective is to further help my community by securing a position that will enable me to continue to fight in a more effective way & to positively affect the lives of everyday people."

positions.summary: Says she would work to repeal New York's sanctuary-state policies.
positions.quote: I will work to remove NYS sanctuary status.

candidates.researchNotes: Marrero has not completed a 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey; the quoted positions above are from her 2024 survey for a different office (State Assembly District 80) and may not reflect any change in her views since. Re-searched 2026-10-19; no website or 2026 statements found. Her 2024 call to vote no on Proposal 1 (Equal Rights Amendment) was removed as an abortion position: her stated objection concerned parental rights and gender identity, not abortion.
